headline: SSGC announces eight-hour daily gas supply schedule for winter
description: Domestic consumers will receive gas during three fixed time slots under new schedule
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) has issued a new gas supply schedule for the winter season, under which domestic consumers will receive gas for only eight hours a day.

According to the company, gas supply timings have been fixed for the morning, afternoon and evening, with the new schedule coming into effect from today.

An SSGC spokesperson said domestic consumers would receive gas from 6:30am to 9am, followed by another supply window from noon to 2:30pm.

Gas will also be available in the evening from 6pm to 9pm.

The company said the schedule had been drawn up to improve gas availability during the winter months, adding that domestic consumers would be given priority in gas distribution.

headline: Minister of Interior and Chairman of the PCB is like a wandering albatross
description: Road closures linked to visiting cricket teams frustrate commuters in Pakistan’s major cities
author: Anjum Ibrahim
article_text:
“It is such a struggle to come to work every day.”

“How come? There is not that much traffic in the federal capital anymore because half of our civil servants paid salaries from our tax rupees stay at home as part of the government’s austerity drive …”

“Yeah due to the Middle East conflict, I had thought that the current round of negotiation was succeeding — JD Vance wrote a less, how can I put it, less IMF type of letter to the Iranians.”

“Where does the IMF come in? Last Iran applied for a Fund loan, 6 billion dollars, was in March 2020 for COVID-19 relief, the first the country requested since almost 1960, and I think it was opposed by the US so …”

“I said JD Vance’s letter was less harsh than the IMF press releases and documents that we in Pakistan are routinely getting under the ongoing Extended Fund Facility programme.”

“Don’t be facetious anyway on Monday the US and Israeli planes attacked some Iranian islands contiguous to the Strait of Hormuz, so much for JD Vance’s less insulting tone …”

“When I said it was a struggle to come to work I wasn’t referring to the price of petrol which the government is considering reducing but … ….”

“I know it is a struggle for you to come to work because your car is old and repairs are costing you a hell of a lot more.”

“That’s true, but the government has already approved or is about to approve used car imports by commercial importers and ….”

“Right so not that either?”

“Nope it’s the dratted cricket teams who have been in the country for over a month. Where ever they go the road blocks are ….”

“I heard that, in Lahore too people are complaining.”

“Must be loyalists of The Man Who Must Remain Nameless, Voiceless and Faceless ….”

“Well the thing is that the dual hatted Minister of Interior and Chairman of the Pakistan Cricket Board is like a wandering albatross, the bird with the largest wing span, and his wing span now extends from Islamabad to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to Punjab’s heartland Lahore and ….”

“Careful my friend.”

“Mian sahib is out of the country ….”

“But a faithful ally Salik Hussain is here.”

“What goes up must come down at some point.”

headline: NAB summons Asad Mahmood in 'illegal appointments' case
description: Former minister asked to appear on November 10 over hirings at Pakistan Post
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) has summoned former federal minister for communications Asad Mahmood, son of Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, in connection with alleged irregularities in recruitment at Pakistan Post.

NAB’s Rawalpindi office has directed Asad Mahmood to appear before its investigation team on November 10 at 11am.

According to a notice issued by te NAB, the bureau is investigating alleged irregularities in appointments made at Pakistan Post during Asad Mahmood’s tenure as communications minister between 2022 and 2023.

The notice states that the Establishment Division had authorised recruitment against 3,938 posts at Pakistan Post. However, 4,252 people were allegedly appointed, exceeding the approved number.

The NAB said that 2,646 appointments were made against posts that had already been abolished, in violation of the directions of a cabinet committee.

The bureau further stated that while recruitment on a contractual basis had been recommended, a large number of permanent appointments were made instead.

The investigation also covers allegations that the appointments placed an additional financial burden on Pakistan Post.

Claims of political affiliations among some selected candidates are also being examined, sources said.

Other allegations include the use of fake and forged documents, recruitment of candidates over the prescribed age limit and violations of the domicile quota during the hiring process.

The NAB has warned that failure to comply with the summons could result in legal action under Section 31 of the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999.

Meanwhile, the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) is also investigating alleged corruption and irregularities in recruitment at Pakistan Post.

The FIA’s Anti-Corruption Circle in Islamabad had separately issued a notice summoning Mahmood to record his statement in connection with the case.

Both agencies are examining allegations of appointments beyond the approved number of vacancies and other suspected violations of recruitment rules.

headline: Unlocking Pakistan’s digital potential
description: Technology transforming economic, social landscape, but gaps in infrastructure remain major hurdle
author: Tariq Khalique
article_text:
A young freelancer sitting in a small town can now design a website for a company in London, communicate with its team online and earn an income without leaving Pakistan. A few years ago, such an opportunity might have seemed out of reach for many young people.

Today, it reflects how technology is changing the country’s economic and social landscape. From digital banking and online businesses to education and public services, technology is creating new possibilities and changing traditional ways of working.

However, the benefits of this transformation are not reaching everyone equally. Limited digital skills, unreliable internet services, inadequate infrastructure and cybersecurity risks continue to hold the country back.

Pakistan’s real challenge is to move beyond adopting modern technology and build a digital environment that is accessible, secure and beneficial to all. If supported by effective policies, investment and a skilled workforce, digital transformation could become an important driver of economic growth, employment and social development.

The idea of digital Pakistan goes beyond introducing new applications or increasing internet usage. It involves creating an environment in which individuals, businesses and government institutions can use technology to work more efficiently and achieve better results.

The growing use of smartphones and digital platforms has already changed how people communicate, shop and conduct business. Small businesses can promote their products through social media, entrepreneurs can establish online stores, and professionals can offer their services to international markets.

These developments demonstrate the potential of technology to support economic growth and encourage innovation.

One of the most visible developments in Pakistan’s digital journey is the growth of mobile banking and online financial services.

In the past, people often had to visit banks to transfer money, pay bills or carry out basic financial transactions.

Today, services such as Easypaisa and JazzCash allow users to send and receive money, pay utility bills and make purchases through their mobile phones.

Digital banking has also made financial services more accessible to people who do not have traditional bank accounts. For small shopkeepers and home-based businesses, these services can save time and simplify daily transactions.

However, greater awareness and stronger security measures are needed to protect users from online fraud and financial scams.

Pakistan’s freelance industry is another example of how digital technology can create economic opportunities. Thousands of young Pakistanis offer services in graphic design, software development, content writing, digital marketing and video editing.

Platforms such as Fiverr and Upwork have enabled skilled individuals to work with clients from different parts of the world. This industry has particular importance in a country where unemployment and limited job opportunities remain serious concerns.

With proper training, reliable infrastructure and better payment facilities, freelancing could become an even stronger source of foreign income for Pakistan. It could also encourage young people to develop professional skills and establish their own businesses.

The education sector has experienced significant changes because of digital technology. Online learning platforms, educational websites and video lectures have made knowledge more accessible.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, schools, colleges and universities relied on online classes to continue their academic activities. Although this transition was difficult for many students, it demonstrated the importance of digital education.

Today, students can use platforms such as YouTube and other learning websites to understand difficult subjects, develop new skills and prepare for examinations.

Digital libraries also provide access to books, research papers and educational material. However, technology should support traditional education rather than replace the role of teachers, classroom interaction and practical learning.

The healthcare sector can also benefit greatly from digital transformation. Telemedicine allows patients to consult doctors through video calls and other online services.

This can be helpful for the people living in remote villages, where specialist doctors and well-equipped hospitals are not easily available.

For example, a patient in a distant area may receive medical advice from a specialist in Karachi, Lahore or Islamabad without travelling long distances. Digital health records can also help hospitals manage patient information more efficiently.

On Tuesday, gold price remained unchanged at Rs412,136.

The international rate of gold was up by $139 to reach $4,035 per ounce.

Meanwhile, the price of silver increased by Rs295 to reach Rs5,663 per tola.

headline: Four oil tankers catch fire after hitting mines in Hormuz: Iran
description: IRGC claims four vessels were destroyed while attempting to cross a restricted passage
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Four oil tankers caught fire after reportedly striking naval mines while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday, amid renewed tensions between Tehran and Washington.

The announcement came a day after US President Donald Trump said American forces had carried out strikes against Iran, following reports of an attack on Qeshm Island, the largest island in the Strait of Hormuz.

According to a statement by the IRGC carried by Iranian state television, four oil tankers attempting to cross a restricted route south of the strait were destroyed after hitting naval mines and remained on fire.

The Guards also said two other vessels had been stopped from proceeding through the waterway, while a drone was shot down over the strait.

Iran maintains control over the Strait of Hormuz, a key international shipping route through which a significant share of the world’s energy supplies passes.

Since the outbreak of the conflict, Tehran has targeted vessels attempting to navigate the waterway without its authorisation.

The war began in February after the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran.

Meanwhile, indirect communications between Washington and Tehran have continued through mediators, although efforts to reach a diplomatic agreement have yet to produce a breakthrough.

Iran has indicated its willingness to reopen the strait, but has made the move conditional on the United States accepting a set of longstanding demands.

Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with Washington, said the country remained prepared for military confrontation, declaring that the Islamic Republic was “ready for battle with its finger on the trigger”.

However, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government was seeking to resolve the crisis through diplomatic engagement.

“No one will benefit from this war” if hostilities resume, Pezeshkian said on Tuesday, as tensions over the strategically important waterway continued.

headline: Democrats reclaim US Senate in blow to President Trump
description: Democrats secure a 53-seat Senate majority and make gains in the House of Representatives
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The Democratic Party has regained control of the US Senate from President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections, while also winning several Republican-held seats in the House of Representatives.

According to The Associated Press, the Democrats’ victory in the Senate has been confirmed, although control of the House remains undecided.

According to the latest election figures released by the AP, Democrats have secured 53 seats in the Senate, while Republicans have won 41.

Democratic candidates have so far secured 213 seats in the House of Representatives, compared with 126 for Republicans.

However, these results cannot be declared final as vote counting is underway in several constituencies.

According to US media projections, Democrats are on course to secure at least 239 seats in the House of Representatives, while Republicans are projected to secure at least 161 seats.

Vote counting continuing in several constituencies, particularly in California and Texas, which have a large number of seats. Counting is also progressing relatively slowly in states such as Maine and Alaska, meaning it could take more time before the final picture emerges.

headline: Deb Haaland makes history as first Native American woman elected governor
description: Haaland defeats Republican Gregg Hull in New Mexico to secure a landmark victory
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Deb Haaland became the first Native American woman to win a governorship after she defeated Republican Gregg Hull in New Mexico in Tuesday’s mid-term elections.

A member of the Laguna Pueblo tribe, Haaland has longstanding ties to New Mexico, where Indigenous communities make up around 12 per cent of the population.

During her campaign, she spoke about the rising cost of living, access to healthcare and problems within the state’s child welfare system. She also criticised President Donald Trump’s policies, referring to her experience opposing his administration during her time in Congress.

Haaland will succeed fellow Democrat Michelle Lujan Grisham, who is barred from seeking another term under state law.

headline: Pakistani-American candidates win seats in US midterm elections
description: Maryam Sabih, Maryam Khan, Saeed Anwar and others secure victories in state legislatures
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Several Pakistani-American candidates have won elections in different US states, securing seats in state legislatures, US media said on Wednesday.

According to reports, a number of candidates of Pakistani origin emerged victorious in Tuesday’s mid-term elections.

Maryam Sabih won a seat in the Pennsylvania State Assembly, while Maryam Khan secured victory in Connecticut’s State Senate.

In another win for the Pakistani-American community, Saeed Anwar was re-elected to the Connecticut State Senate.

Texas also saw victories for two Pakistani-American lawmakers. Salman Bhojani was re-elected to the state House of Representatives, securing 67 per cent of the vote.

Suleman Lalani also retained his seat in the Texas House of Representatives.

In Georgia, Farooq Mughal won the state House of Representatives election from District 105 with 60.8 per cent of the vote.

However, not all Pakistani-American candidates managed to win. Republican candidate Imtiaz Muhammad lost his race for the Florida State House of Representatives.

headline: OpenAI faces fresh scrutiny over internal security risks
description: Former employees say OpenAI overlooked security warnings for years
author: Reuters
article_text:
When OpenAI disclosed in October that it found a recording device planted in an executive conference room, several former employees had the same reaction — they were not surprised.

Even before OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022, some company staffers raised concerns internally about its security practices, according to five people familiar with the matter.

Employees shared their concerns with top OpenAI leaders ​and the board of directors, the people said, adding that some staffers came away from those interactions concluding that management was more focused on keeping pace with competitors like Google and Anthropic than on security.

These workers argued that OpenAI’s controls were so lax ‌that outsiders, including foreign governments, could obtain sensitive information about the AI lab’s technology with relative ease, the people said.

For example, anybody at OpenAI who could access its code could see the technical details underlying many company projects.

OpenAI has begun to shift strategy to address security issues, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Thibault Sottiaux, a senior executive overseeing product development, has recently taken charge of an internal initiative to secure OpenAI’s internal systems, they said.

In August, Sottiaux, who goes by “Tibo,” reassigned a quarter of OpenAI’s production engineers to improve its security infrastructure, one of the people said.

The internal warnings, including years of employee complaints to leadership about internal vulnerabilities, certain details of which have not been previously reported, shed light ​on a tension within the AI field.

Since ChatGPT launched in late 2022, AI technology has become a strategic asset for the US, putting pressure on American companies to protect their technology from foreign rivals.

But adding security layers can also delay the process of advancing AI technology and possibly ​complicate OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s plans for massive initial public offerings that would make them among the most valuable companies in the world.

Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who resigned from the company in April of this year, wrote in ⁠a post on X that with competition so tense, AI leaders “can’t sacrifice velocity for security. It is more important to them to move fast than to be secure, even from our greatest national adversaries.”

When asked about employees’ concerns and their view that management did not act on these issues, OpenAI spokesperson Elana Widmann ​said that OpenAI is one of the most targeted organisations in the world.

As a result, the company invests heavily in its security program to protect against attacks from insiders, cybercriminals and nation-states, she said.

“Protecting our technology, data, and people is a responsibility we take seriously and a matter of national importance,” Widmann said.

“The ​actions we’ve taken recently show that the program is doing its job: identifying risks and responding decisively. We’ll keep strengthening our defences as technology and threats evolve.”

Research widely available

On October 13, the Justice Department said US federal agents arrested a Saudi national and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording device, concealed in toilet paper, in an executive conference room.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was an OpenAI engineer at the time.

Alfozan also used an AI tool meant for OpenAI employees to find internal documentation about executives visiting Saudi Arabia and which OpenAI officials were most likely to attend meetings with Saudi ministers, according to a court filing.

Alfozan was in regular contact with a Saudi royal who tried to recruit him for a new AI ​venture launching in Saudi Arabia. Lawyers for Alfozan did not respond to a request for comment.

Some employees have long been concerned about the wide availability of information within OpenAI, the five people familiar with OpenAI’s practices said.

Anybody at OpenAI who could access its code could also see the details underlying many of the ​company’s projects, including sensitive ones unrelated to an employee’s work.

That is because OpenAI stored most of its code in a single repository, known in the industry as a “monorepo,” the people said.

The monorepo was dense and complicated, which may have deterred some would-be attackers in the past. Now, AI agents can sift through that amount of material.

In ‌the past, OpenAI has ⁠kept much of its research documentation on GitHub and Slack, raising concerns among some employees that motivated actors could still find crucial information, the five people said. But one of the sources and OpenAI said the company has restricted access to sensitive work.

OpenAI emphasised that much of its most sensitive work is held in separate code repositories with strict access controls.

And it said the monorepo does not contain all of its code or critical details of the company’s models, including the numerical values that determine how a model behaves, known as the model weights.

Another issue is that OpenAI had not done regular security reviews of its internal tools, such as the so-called sandboxes where researchers stress-test new models, three people familiar with the company’s practices said.

Employees often modified those tools for their work, but those changes were not always tested for security problems, leaving them potentially vulnerable to attacks from outsiders, the three people said.

The company said it has a strong approach ​to security under its chief information security officer, Dane Stuckey, who joined in ​October 2024. OpenAI said it now conducts regular security reviews of ⁠its internal tooling.

Open debate versus security

OpenAI is not the only AI company to face security problems.

In January, a federal jury in San Francisco convicted a former Google employee who was arrested in March 2024 on charges of stealing thousands of pages of confidential information about Google’s AI technology on behalf of China.

In late October, a cybersecurity startup called Cathedral Systems said it hacked into Anthropic’s systems and gained access to Slack channels where employees discussed sensitive model details.

An Anthropic spokesperson said ​the data accessed included some business contact information for customers and partners as well as a set of basic user account records. Cathedral’s CEO did not respond to a request for comment.

OpenAI and Anthropic have tried to ​maintain a more open research culture to both ⁠attract employees and foster creativity that can lead to breakthroughs.

The AI field is rooted in academia, where machine-learning scientists have openly discussed their research.

Some OpenAI employees are increasingly worried about this approach as AI grows more capable, according to the five people.

In 2023, Leopold Aschenbrenner, then an OpenAI researcher, wrote an internal memo titled “OpenAI is China’s leading AI lab” about his concerns that China could infiltrate OpenAI and study its technology, three people familiar with the matter said.

Aschenbrenner shared that memo with some board members later that year after an outsider hacked into OpenAI and took details about its GPT-4 model.

OpenAI said the hacker accessed only Slack channels available to the whole company.

Security concerns ⁠within OpenAI flared up ​again this summer when OpenAI agents being tested hacked into the AI company Hugging Face, an incident that prompted scrutiny from state, local and federal officials, including the White House.

Cybersecurity firm Hacktron ​AI said, opens new tab three of its researchers used a rival AI model from Anthropic in July to break into ChatGPT accounts belonging to multiple OpenAI employees and gained access to some internal OpenAI systems, including its monorepo. The incident exposed how advanced AI can now put the AI companies themselves at risk of attack.

OpenAI’s Widmann said the company thanked the researchers for sharing their findings and that it ​took steps to minimise the risk of similar attacks in the future.

After Reuters sought comment for this story, OpenAI said on Monday in a blog post that it is planning its “next internal security sprint” to beef up its defences.

article_html:
When OpenAI disclosed in October that it found a recording device planted in an executive conference room, several former employees had the same reaction — they were not surprised.

Even before OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022, some company staffers raised concerns internally about its security practices, according to five people familiar with the matter.

Employees shared their concerns with top OpenAI leaders ​and the board of directors, the people said, adding that some staffers came away from those interactions concluding that management was more focused on keeping pace with competitors like Google and Anthropic than on security.

These workers argued that OpenAI’s controls were so lax ‌that outsiders, including foreign governments, could obtain sensitive information about the AI lab’s technology with relative ease, the people said.

For example, anybody at OpenAI who could access its code could see the technical details underlying many company projects.

OpenAI has begun to shift strategy to address security issues, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Thibault Sottiaux, a senior executive overseeing product development, has recently taken charge of an internal initiative to secure OpenAI’s internal systems, they said.

In August, Sottiaux, who goes by “Tibo,” reassigned a quarter of OpenAI’s production engineers to improve its security infrastructure, one of the people said.

The internal warnings, including years of employee complaints to leadership about internal vulnerabilities, certain details of which have not been previously reported, shed light ​on a tension within the AI field.

Since ChatGPT launched in late 2022, AI technology has become a strategic asset for the US, putting pressure on American companies to protect their technology from foreign rivals.

But adding security layers can also delay the process of advancing AI technology and possibly ​complicate OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s plans for massive initial public offerings that would make them among the most valuable companies in the world.

Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who resigned from the company in April of this year, wrote in ⁠a post on X that with competition so tense, AI leaders “can’t sacrifice velocity for security. It is more important to them to move fast than to be secure, even from our greatest national adversaries.”

When asked about employees’ concerns and their view that management did not act on these issues, OpenAI spokesperson Elana Widmann ​said that OpenAI is one of the most targeted organisations in the world.

As a result, the company invests heavily in its security program to protect against attacks from insiders, cybercriminals and nation-states, she said.

“Protecting our technology, data, and people is a responsibility we take seriously and a matter of national importance,” Widmann said.

“The ​actions we’ve taken recently show that the program is doing its job: identifying risks and responding decisively. We’ll keep strengthening our defences as technology and threats evolve.”

Research widely available

On October 13, the Justice Department said US federal agents arrested a Saudi national and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording device, concealed in toilet paper, in an executive conference room.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was an OpenAI engineer at the time.

Alfozan also used an AI tool meant for OpenAI employees to find internal documentation about executives visiting Saudi Arabia and which OpenAI officials were most likely to attend meetings with Saudi ministers, according to a court filing.

Alfozan was in regular contact with a Saudi royal who tried to recruit him for a new AI ​venture launching in Saudi Arabia. Lawyers for Alfozan did not respond to a request for comment.

Some employees have long been concerned about the wide availability of information within OpenAI, the five people familiar with OpenAI’s practices said.

Anybody at OpenAI who could access its code could also see the details underlying many of the ​company’s projects, including sensitive ones unrelated to an employee’s work.

That is because OpenAI stored most of its code in a single repository, known in the industry as a “monorepo,” the people said.

The monorepo was dense and complicated, which may have deterred some would-be attackers in the past. Now, AI agents can sift through that amount of material.

In ‌the past, OpenAI has ⁠kept much of its research documentation on GitHub and Slack, raising concerns among some employees that motivated actors could still find crucial information, the five people said. But one of the sources and OpenAI said the company has restricted access to sensitive work.

OpenAI emphasised that much of its most sensitive work is held in separate code repositories with strict access controls.

And it said the monorepo does not contain all of its code or critical details of the company’s models, including the numerical values that determine how a model behaves, known as the model weights.

Another issue is that OpenAI had not done regular security reviews of its internal tools, such as the so-called sandboxes where researchers stress-test new models, three people familiar with the company’s practices said.

Employees often modified those tools for their work, but those changes were not always tested for security problems, leaving them potentially vulnerable to attacks from outsiders, the three people said.

The company said it has a strong approach ​to security under its chief information security officer, Dane Stuckey, who joined in ​October 2024. OpenAI said it now conducts regular security reviews of ⁠its internal tooling.

Open debate versus security

OpenAI is not the only AI company to face security problems.

In January, a federal jury in San Francisco convicted a former Google employee who was arrested in March 2024 on charges of stealing thousands of pages of confidential information about Google’s AI technology on behalf of China.

In late October, a cybersecurity startup called Cathedral Systems said it hacked into Anthropic’s systems and gained access to Slack channels where employees discussed sensitive model details.

An Anthropic spokesperson said ​the data accessed included some business contact information for customers and partners as well as a set of basic user account records. Cathedral’s CEO did not respond to a request for comment.

OpenAI and Anthropic have tried to ​maintain a more open research culture to both ⁠attract employees and foster creativity that can lead to breakthroughs.

The AI field is rooted in academia, where machine-learning scientists have openly discussed their research.

Some OpenAI employees are increasingly worried about this approach as AI grows more capable, according to the five people.

In 2023, Leopold Aschenbrenner, then an OpenAI researcher, wrote an internal memo titled “OpenAI is China’s leading AI lab” about his concerns that China could infiltrate OpenAI and study its technology, three people familiar with the matter said.

Aschenbrenner shared that memo with some board members later that year after an outsider hacked into OpenAI and took details about its GPT-4 model.

OpenAI said the hacker accessed only Slack channels available to the whole company.

Security concerns ⁠within OpenAI flared up ​again this summer when OpenAI agents being tested hacked into the AI company Hugging Face, an incident that prompted scrutiny from state, local and federal officials, including the White House.

Cybersecurity firm Hacktron ​AI said, opens new tab three of its researchers used a rival AI model from Anthropic in July to break into ChatGPT accounts belonging to multiple OpenAI employees and gained access to some internal OpenAI systems, including its monorepo. The incident exposed how advanced AI can now put the AI companies themselves at risk of attack.

OpenAI’s Widmann said the company thanked the researchers for sharing their findings and that it ​took steps to minimise the risk of similar attacks in the future.

After Reuters sought comment for this story, OpenAI said on Monday in a blog post that it is planning its “next internal security sprint” to beef up its defences.

headline: Iran, US still far apart on deal; Trump says ready but in no hurry for strikes
description: Tehran won't accept 'excessive' US demands, Iranian official says
author: Reuters
article_text:
Iran and the United States are still far from a deal to end their war, a senior Iranian official told ​Reuters on Tuesday, as US President Donald Trump declined to rule out a resumption of US combat operations after the elections in the United States.

Trump made his comments in separate interviews as Americans ‌voted in pivotal midterm elections in which the unpopular Iran war has been a key factor and as mediator Qatar stepped up efforts to avert a renewed escalation.

Overnight, the United States carried out “defensive” strikes on Iran’s Qeshm island, targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets, a US official said. Another official said the strikes appeared limited and did not signal a return to major combat operations.

Trump on Tuesday renewed warnings of military action in an interview with the Fox News Channel. “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people,” he said. “If we have to, we’ll have to.”

In ​an interview with the Financial Times, Trump suggested he was content with the state of the standoff with Iran.

“We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute ​telephone interview.

The FT said it asked Trump about what it called “strong hints” by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that there would be an attack later this week.

“I’m ready, ⁠we’re ready. We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it,” he replied.

Trump told the FT that indirect negotiations with Iran about its stockpile of enriched uranium were ongoing. “We’re having ​discussions, and we’ll see how that all works out,” he said.

Also on Tuesday, Trump made a surprise announcement of a deal with Netanyahu under which Washington would stop $4 billion in annual funding to Israel after this year, but would ​sell weapons to its close Middle East ally. The remarks appeared aimed at swaying voters unhappy with US support for Israel.

Fears have grown that the conflict launched by the United States and Israel in February could flare up again after Tuesday’s midterms.

“Mediators are working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington,” the senior Iranian official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Monday night for talks on a version of a draft US-Iran deal discussed over the past eight days.

“Tehran’s conditions must be met ​if the US wants Hormuz reopened,” the Iranian official cautioned, referring to Iranian demands including waiving oil sanctions, ending the US naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian funds.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, later said the ​US response to Iranian demands “was not convincing”, adding that Washington “must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them”.

“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened,” he wrote on X.

‘We cannot lose hope’

Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari ‌said both the ⁠United States and Iran were reviewing proposals put forward by mediators. While the Qatari team that travelled to Tehran had returned to Doha, talks were continuing.

“There are intensive joint regional efforts underway to avoid escalation,” he told a news briefing, adding that Qatar remained hopeful a deal could still be reached to pave the way for future negotiations.

“If there were no glimmer of hope, there would be no negotiations… and as a mediator, we cannot lose hope,” he said.

An official briefed on the talks said feedback from Washington and Tehran was expected within the next 36 hours.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters later on Tuesday that there is no deadline for exchanging messages with Washington through mediators or reviewing ​responses.

‘Forceful response’

The senior Iranian official said Tehran would not ​accept Washington’s “excessive demands” and that nuclear talks could ⁠begin only after Iran’s conditions were met.

Tehran would respond forcefully, in the region and beyond, to US strikes, the official added.

Oil prices slipped in early trade on Wednesday as investors awaited the results of the midterm elections and their potential impact on peace talks, even after industry data showed US crude stocks unexpectedly fell last week.

Iran’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer ​Qalibaf said the ball was in Washington’s court after a “strong and rational response” from Tehran.

“The enemy seeks to force the Iranian nation into submission through threats and military ​action, but they are sorely mistaken; ⁠Iran will not submit,” Qalibaf said. He said Tehran’s response to any US miscalculation would be unpredictable and unconstrained by geography.

The head of Iran’s armed forces general staff, Ali Abdollahi, said Iran’s military was updating target lists that included US and Israeli assets and would respond immediately to any threat.

Iran and the United States are still far from a deal to end their war, a senior Iranian official told ​Reuters on Tuesday, as US President Donald Trump declined to rule out a resumption of US combat operations after the elections in the United States.

Trump made his comments in separate interviews as Americans ‌voted in pivotal midterm elections in which the unpopular Iran war has been a key factor and as mediator Qatar stepped up efforts to avert a renewed escalation.

Overnight, the United States carried out “defensive” strikes on Iran’s Qeshm island, targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets, a US official said. Another official said the strikes appeared limited and did not signal a return to major combat operations.

Trump on Tuesday renewed warnings of military action in an interview with the Fox News Channel. “I’m not looking to … kill lots of people,” he said. “If we have to, we’ll have to.”

In ​an interview with the Financial Times, Trump suggested he was content with the state of the standoff with Iran.

“We seem to be getting everything we want,” the paper quoted him as saying in a six-minute ​telephone interview.

The FT said it asked Trump about what it called “strong hints” by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that there would be an attack later this week.

“I’m ready, ⁠we’re ready. We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it,” he replied.

Trump told the FT that indirect negotiations with Iran about its stockpile of enriched uranium were ongoing. “We’re having ​discussions, and we’ll see how that all works out,” he said.

Also on Tuesday, Trump made a surprise announcement of a deal with Netanyahu under which Washington would stop $4 billion in annual funding to Israel after this year, but would ​sell weapons to its close Middle East ally. The remarks appeared aimed at swaying voters unhappy with US support for Israel.

Fears have grown that the conflict launched by the United States and Israel in February could flare up again after Tuesday’s midterms.

“Mediators are working hard to narrow gaps between Tehran and Washington,” the senior Iranian official said, speaking on condition of anonymity. Qatari mediators travelled to Tehran on Monday night for talks on a version of a draft US-Iran deal discussed over the past eight days.

“Tehran’s conditions must be met ​if the US wants Hormuz reopened,” the Iranian official cautioned, referring to Iranian demands including waiving oil sanctions, ending the US naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian funds.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, later said the ​US response to Iranian demands “was not convincing”, adding that Washington “must fully and explicitly address Iran’s seven conditions and act upon them”.

“Only in this case will the Strait of Hormuz be reopened,” he wrote on X.

‘We cannot lose hope’

Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari ‌said both the ⁠United States and Iran were reviewing proposals put forward by mediators. While the Qatari team that travelled to Tehran had returned to Doha, talks were continuing.

“There are intensive joint regional efforts underway to avoid escalation,” he told a news briefing, adding that Qatar remained hopeful a deal could still be reached to pave the way for future negotiations.

“If there were no glimmer of hope, there would be no negotiations… and as a mediator, we cannot lose hope,” he said.

An official briefed on the talks said feedback from Washington and Tehran was expected within the next 36 hours.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters later on Tuesday that there is no deadline for exchanging messages with Washington through mediators or reviewing ​responses.

‘Forceful response’

The senior Iranian official said Tehran would not ​accept Washington’s “excessive demands” and that nuclear talks could ⁠begin only after Iran’s conditions were met.

Tehran would respond forcefully, in the region and beyond, to US strikes, the official added.

Oil prices slipped in early trade on Wednesday as investors awaited the results of the midterm elections and their potential impact on peace talks, even after industry data showed US crude stocks unexpectedly fell last week.

Iran’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer ​Qalibaf said the ball was in Washington’s court after a “strong and rational response” from Tehran.

“The enemy seeks to force the Iranian nation into submission through threats and military ​action, but they are sorely mistaken; ⁠Iran will not submit,” Qalibaf said. He said Tehran’s response to any US miscalculation would be unpredictable and unconstrained by geography.

The head of Iran’s armed forces general staff, Ali Abdollahi, said Iran’s military was updating target lists that included US and Israeli assets and would respond immediately to any threat.

Hardline newspaper Kayhan said on Tuesday that US facilities in Britain, Italy, Greece, Romania, Albania and Cyprus could be targeted in the event of renewed war.

Iranian-Saudi talks

Alongside indirect exchanges between Tehran and Washington, regional powers ⁠are pursuing diplomatic ​efforts to prevent further escalation. The conflict has also widened, with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis stepping up attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas ​Araqchi said on Tuesday that talks with Saudi Arabia were continuing to seek new regional security arrangements that would exclude foreign military involvement.

Last week, senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian counterparts in Tehran, the first such high-level contacts since August.

headline: International politicians react to Democrats winning US midterms
description: Governments and political leaders weigh the potential impact on global trade, security and energy prices
author: Reuters
article_text:
Governments and politicians around the world reacted to the Democrats winning the US midterm elections, a result that could have major implications for global trade, security and energy prices.

Here is a selection of the reactions:

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf on X

“Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse ​this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve ​international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes ⁠with a Nightmare.”

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on X

“Yesterday, the American people voted against policies that only serve to impoverish people. Against hatred. Against sexism. Against climate denial and against the privileges of the elites.

“It happened in Brazil. It has just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain.”

Ines Schwerdtner, joint leader of Germany’s left party:

“This is a crashing defeat for the global Right.”

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere

“This is a powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters.

“Voices are now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate ‌and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy.”

Taiwanese Foreign Ministry statement

“The Ministry of Foreign Affairs continues to closely monitor developments in the US midterm elections. Our country’s policy toward the United States has always been guided by the principles of non-partisanship, building broad-based goodwill, and active engagement, and has long enjoyed the consistent support of parties in the US Congress and the executive branch. Building on this foundation, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs will continue to deepen comprehensive cooperation with the United States across various fields —including security, trade, technology, and education — to ensure that the US Congress and local governments continue to prioritise and support US-Taiwan relations and issues ​of mutual concern.”

South African President Cyril Ramaphosa

Ramaphosa told reporters the results will “introduce a new era in world relations.”

“We have seen that the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken.”

European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldermose on X

“Not because everything now changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and relations with the rest of the world.”

“But the EU must ⁠continue the course of standing stronger and standing on its own two feet. That’s not up for debate.”

Greek government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis

“Greek-American relations will remain strong. The United States is our strategic ally, and this will continue for major projects and all major ​agreements. Nothing will be affected by this outcome. It is obvious that we respect every outcome; the conclusions are clear.”

“Beyond that, what I can tell you is that it appears that on the key committees there will be individuals with whom the Greek government has very good relations, and ​that is important for the country.”

Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov

“Let’s wait for the final results. The Democratic Party leadership’s approach to relations with Russia is sharply negative. There is nothing new about that.”

“Our principled and consistent line regarding Ukraine — as well as our foreign policy in general — is not based on short-term considerations and, naturally, does not depend on the fluctuations of the political barometer in other countries. We will continue our work in accordance with the directives of the President of the Russian Federation.”

Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara

“Regardless of the outcome of this election, ​the Japan-US alliance is the cornerstone of Japan’s foreign and security policy.

“As the international situation becomes turbulent and increasingly uncertain, a strong Japan-US alliance is essential for maximising Japan’s national interests and for peace and stability in the international community.”

French Finance Minister Roland Lescure

“Either he decides to rise above the fray — acknowledging that changes are necessary, particularly regarding gasoline prices, which directly affect people — and, I might add, he tones down his international involvement; or he does not.”

“Frankly, this is something we will need to keep an eye on in the coming days.”

Co-leader of German far-right party AFD, Alice Weidel

“Trump had promised his voters not to pursue an interventionist foreign policy… This broken promise has now come back to haunt the Republicans.”

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis

“I think the outcome was as expected, although of course the Democrats’ victory is huge. Even the Republican stronghold of Texas fell, and in some places Democrats gained positions after decades.

“In my view, this means that until the end of President Trump’s term, it will be all about impeachment and vetoes, and a certain kind of paralysis. On the other hand, President Trump will almost certainly continue to do exactly as he pleases.

Let’s hope he finally returns to his promise to end the war in Ukraine and resolve the conflict in the Strait of Hormuz.“

Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken on X

“Governing in the United States will be almost impossible in the coming years given the level of internal division and polarisation. As a European politician, I will mainly look, of course, to trade policies, support to Ukraine and NATO.”

Jordan Bardella, President of Far-right opposition party national rally in France

headline: KSE-100 surges nearly 4,000 points on geopolitical optimism
description: Institutional buying and hopes of easing oil prices and US-Iran negotiations drive the benchmark index up 2.38%
author: Business Recorder
article_text:
The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) witnessed a strong bullish session on Wednesday, with the benchmark KSE-100 Index gaining nearly 4,000 points amid institutional buying and improving sentiment over geopolitical developments following US midterm election results.

The benchmark index opened on a positive note and maintained its upward momentum throughout the session. It initially surged sharply, crossing the 170,000-point mark before witnessing some consolidation and a brief dip around 11am.

However, buying interest returned around midday, allowing the index to resume its upward trajectory. The rally gained further momentum, with the benchmark extending its gains and approaching the intraday high of 172,286.99 towards the end of the session.

At close, the KSE-100 Index settled at 172,013.48, up 3,994.62 points or 2.38%.

“Buying has mainly come from institutions, particularly mutual funds, which is driving the interest we are seeing,” Sana Tawfik, Head of Research at Arif Habib Limited (AHL), said.

“Secondly, oil prices had risen to around $103 and have stabilised at that level, which has also helped sentiment,” she added.

Globally, the analyst said, the US market is closely watching geopolitical developments.

“One is the US election, where the unofficial numbers coming in so far show a visible shift. The other is the US-Iran talks, where the US has sent a draft.

All these factors together are supporting the market at the moment.”

Similarly, Saad Hanif, Head of Research at Ismail Iqbal Securities, said that the rally is partly tied to the US midterm elections.

“Investors read a Democratic sweep as positive for regional geopolitics, expecting a more measured approach from Washington and a stronger preference for negotiation over confrontation in the region.

“That outlook is feeding expectations of lower global oil prices and easing inflation, which is a favourable backdrop for Pakistan’s market and has lifted sentiment, taking the PSX up 4,000 points,” he said.

headline: Govt readies winter plan to secure LPG, LNG supplies: PM
description: Cabinet told energy needs are reviewed every two to three days; LPG sector monopoly ended
author: APP
article_text:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said on Wednesday the government is making all-out efforts to ensure adequate supplies of liquefied natural gas (LNG), liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) and oil this winter, despite rising international prices and disruption to maritime routes.

Chairing a federal cabinet meeting, he said the government is meeting every two to three days to review energy requirements and finalise contingency and coordination plans. He added that every effort would be made to keep power plants running and limit the impact of higher energy prices on the public.

The prime minister announced that the decades-old monopoly in the LPG sector had ended.

Locally produced LPG will now be allocated through competitive, supervised auctions, while importing companies must follow prescribed procedures. Revenue from the auctions will go to the national exchequer and be used to fund subsidies and relief for ordinary citizens.

On crude prices, he said Petroleum Minister Ali Pervaiz Malik, his team, OGRA and the relevant committee had acted in a timely manner by asking refineries to share their windfall profits. The move helped avoid passing a proposed Rs15 per litre increase in petrol prices on to consumers.

The prime minister said the government’s subsidy programme, which has reached around 15 million people, will continue until at least the end of December. About Rs28 billion has been spent so far, benefiting an estimated 75 million people when family members are counted.

He said the programme was running transparently, but intelligence agencies had found irregularities at a few petrol pumps. He directed the petroleum minister to shut them down and impose heavy fines on those involved.

Regional instability, he said, was the main driver of the sharp rise in global crude prices, and Pakistan was working to promote peace and stability.

He cited recent diplomatic engagements, including two Pakistani delegation visits to Tehran, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir’s visit, and visits to Pakistan by the Saudi defence minister and Turkish official Ibrahim Kalin.

He said these had produced constructive talks on easing regional tensions and advancing the proposed trilateral arrangement between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia.

On security, the prime minister said the government had finalised a Rs160 billion development and security package for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

He expressed confidence that the sacrifices of the armed forces and law enforcement agencies, together with better arrangements and provincial cooperation, would help eliminate terrorism.

He said the people of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan had suffered greatly from terrorism and reiterated the government’s resolve to eradicate it permanently.

headline: Iran warns of wider war if US attacks after Trump poll rout
description: Supreme leader says Washington’s hostility will not change with Trump’s midterm defeat, as mediators push for an interim deal
author: AFP
article_text:
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned on Wednesday that the Middle East war would widen if the US resumes its attacks, dismissing hopes of a policy shift in Washington after midterm elections dealt a blow to President Donald Trump.

Trump has recently threatened to renew the war against Iran amid similar rhetoric from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, but on Tuesday he suffered a resounding defeat in polls that will strip his Republicans of control over Congress.

The results could constrain Trump’s ability to enact his agenda, though the president retains the power to order new strikes.

“Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a written statement Wednesday.

He also warned that if the United States did choose further military action, the scope of the war would widen, without elaborating.

Khamenei has yet to appear in public since he took power in March following the killing of his father and predecessor in US-Israeli strikes, and has communicated through written messages.

Earlier, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with the US, said Americans had voted against war in the midterms.

“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” he posted on X.

“If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” Ghalibaf said.

Iran’s judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei also hailed the election results, saying Trump had been “defeated both militarily and politically”.

The war has proved unpopular among the US public, who have seen the cost of living rise after a spike in energy prices caused by the war.

Trump on Tuesday acknowledged the conflict may have played a part in the defeat of his Republican Party.

“I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time, people understood the importance of what I’ve done,” Trump told Fox News.

On Tuesday, the US launched strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with Iranian state media reporting five explosions in rapid succession.

“They built an anti-aircraft facility… As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night very nicely,” Trump told US media, but he called it a “minor attack”.

‘Locked and loaded’

Earlier this week, the president said he still had to “take care” of one or two targets, including so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.

However, he told the Financial Times on Tuesday that a full-scale resumption of war may not be necessary.

“We seem to be getting everything we want,” he said. “I’m ready, we’re ready. We’re locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it.”

The president’s remarks come with diplomatic efforts by mediators in full swing in an attempt to prevent any resumption of fighting.

On Tuesday, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government was still trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue.

Pezeshkian said Iran’s supreme leader had granted the government new powers to negotiate on issues previously off-limits.

Qatar, a mediator in the protracted wrangling, said it remained hopeful of an interim deal.

Both sides “are currently reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented”, Qatari foreign ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari told reporters.

China also said Wednesday that avoiding a return to hostilities was a top priority in its diplomatic efforts with the countries.

The war, triggered in February when the US and Israel pummelled Iran in a massive wave of strikes, has been at a stalemate for months.

Iranian officials have repeatedly warned of wide-ranging retaliation if Washington resumes the war.

The results could constrain Trump’s ability to enact his agenda, though the president retains the power to order new strikes.

“Those who still harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system might change through partisan or factional shifts, or who imagine that making concessions to the United States can dissuade it from hostility towards the Iranian nation, are seriously mistaken,” Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a written statement Wednesday.

He also warned that if the United States did choose further military action, the scope of the war would widen, without elaborating.

Khamenei has yet to appear in public since he took power in March following the killing of his father and predecessor in US-Israeli strikes, and has communicated through written messages.

“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” he posted on X.

“They built an anti-aircraft facility… As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night very nicely,” Trump told US media, but he called it a “minor attack”.

headline: Federal cabinet approves new currency note designs, Rs10 coin
description: New banknotes will feature enhanced security features and durable materials to curb counterfeiting and extend their lifespan
author: Naveed Akbar
article_text:
The federal cabinet on Wednesday approved new designs for Pakistan’s currency notes and the introduction of a Rs10 coin to replace the existing Rs10 banknote.

The decisions were taken at a cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, which also discussed administrative matters in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and defence cooperation between Pakistan and Kuwait, among other issues.

The cabinet approved the new currency note designs on the recommendation of the Ministry of Finance. It was briefed in detail on the proposed designs and the process followed for their preparation.

Officials told the meeting that suggestions had been invited from artists and designers across the country to develop the new designs.

A cabinet committee formed by the prime minister had also held detailed consultations with all relevant stakeholders on the proposed designs, the briefing said.

The new banknotes will incorporate modern security features to prevent counterfeiting. Advanced materials will also be used in their production to improve durability and extend their usable lifespan.

Separately, the cabinet approved the introduction of a Rs10 coin in place of the existing Rs10 banknote.

headline: Thousands mock Trump's midterm setback at Tehran rally
description: Annual anti-American rally marks 1979 embassy seizure a day after Republicans lose control of Congress
author: AFP
article_text:
Hours after US voters stripped President Donald Trump’s Republicans of control of Congress, partly over the Iran war, thousands gathered Wednesday outside the former US embassy in Tehran for an annual anti-American rally.

Chants of “Death to America” and “Death to Israel” echoed through central Tehran as demonstrators waved Iranian flags and carried banners denouncing Washington and Israel.

One banner depicted Trump as a blood-stained bulldog on a leash held by a devil-like figure resembling Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Others called for revenge for the slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, killed by the US-Israeli strikes that sparked the regional war in late February.

Towering over the crowd was a giant display declaring: “The people of Iran set the price.”

Beside it, black oil barrels stretched across a map of the world, a symbol of soaring energy prices since the war erupted and Iran asserted control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route.

“America has been tormenting us for years, but it has not been able to do anything to Iran,” said Mahmoudkhani, 40, who attended the rally marking the 1979 seizure of the embassy and the hostage crisis that followed.

The rally came a day after Trump’s blistering US midterm bashing, widely viewed as a referendum on his turbulent second term, with frustration over living costs, a rollercoaster of tariffs and the conflict with Iran playing a major role.

“We are not happy about the surge in oil prices,” said Mahmoudkhani, who gave only her last name.

“But there is some satisfaction in knowing we are no longer living this torment alone. We, alone, have been suffering under sanctions for so many years.”

Tehran claiming control over Hormuz has disrupted shipping through one of the world’s most important energy chokepoints, while Washington has responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Majid Heidari, a 62-year-old fabric producer, argued the resulting rise in oil prices had “impacted the American vote”.

“When Europe and the US unite against us, we must use our tool (closing Hormuz),” he said.

“There is nothing we can do but put some pressure on governments by making their own people feel the consequences.”

Still, he doubted the US election result would really change much for ordinary Iranians.

Mohammad, a 42-year-old civil servant, shared this view.

“I believe whether it is the Democrats or the Republicans, there is no difference for us,” he said.

“The US government’s approach towards the Iranian people has unfortunately remained the same over the past 50 years.”

‘No to war’

In Tehran’s first official reaction to the vote, its chief negotiator in talks with Washington, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, hailed the outcome.

“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” he wrote on X.

Efforts led by Qatar and Pakistan to broker a deal between Tehran and Washington have made little progress amid mounting concern about a return to fighting.

The annual rally marks the storming of the US embassy in Tehran in November 1979, months after the Islamic Revolution that toppled the US-backed shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.

The students who seized the embassy demanded the return of the shah, who was receiving cancer treatment in the US.

They held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days, and diplomatic ties between the two countries were severed in 1980.

Iranian authorities have since turned the anniversary into an annual display of defiance against what they call Western “arrogance”.

“Crown of arrogance on an empty brain,” read one banner on Wednesday, showing a crown dripping with blood.

“America is the enemy regardless,” said Bagheri, a 35-year-old school principal who gave only her surname.

“It makes no difference who is in charge in the United States.”

Hours after US voters stripped President Donald Trump’s Republicans of control of Congress, partly over the Iran war, thousands gathered Wednesday outside the former US embassy in Tehran for an annual anti-American rally.

Chants of “Death to America” and “Death to Israel” echoed through central Tehran as demonstrators waved Iranian flags and carried banners denouncing Washington and Israel.

One banner depicted Trump as a blood-stained bulldog on a leash held by a devil-like figure resembling Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Others called for revenge for the slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, killed by the US-Israeli strikes that sparked the regional war in late February.

Towering over the crowd was a giant display declaring: “The people of Iran set the price.”

Beside it, black oil barrels stretched across a map of the world, a symbol of soaring energy prices since the war erupted and Iran asserted control over the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route.

“America has been tormenting us for years, but it has not been able to do anything to Iran,” said Mahmoudkhani, 40, who attended the rally marking the 1979 seizure of the embassy and the hostage crisis that followed.

The rally came a day after Trump’s blistering US midterm bashing, widely viewed as a referendum on his turbulent second term, with frustration over living costs, a rollercoaster of tariffs and the conflict with Iran playing a major role.

“We are not happy about the surge in oil prices,” said Mahmoudkhani, who gave only her last name.

“But there is some satisfaction in knowing we are no longer living this torment alone. We, alone, have been suffering under sanctions for so many years.”

Tehran claiming control over Hormuz has disrupted shipping through one of the world’s most important energy chokepoints, while Washington has responded with a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Majid Heidari, a 62-year-old fabric producer, argued the resulting rise in oil prices had “impacted the American vote”.

“When Europe and the US unite against us, we must use our tool (closing Hormuz),” he said.

“There is nothing we can do but put some pressure on governments by making their own people feel the consequences.”

Still, he doubted the US election result would really change much for ordinary Iranians.

Mohammad, a 42-year-old civil servant, shared this view.

“I believe whether it is the Democrats or the Republicans, there is no difference for us,” he said.

“The US government’s approach towards the Iranian people has unfortunately remained the same over the past 50 years.”

‘No to war’

In Tehran’s first official reaction to the vote, its chief negotiator in talks with Washington, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, hailed the outcome.

“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” he wrote on X.

Efforts led by Qatar and Pakistan to broker a deal between Tehran and Washington have made little progress amid mounting concern about a return to fighting.

The annual rally marks the storming of the US embassy in Tehran in November 1979, months after the Islamic Revolution that toppled the US-backed shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.

The students who seized the embassy demanded the return of the shah, who was receiving cancer treatment in the US.

They held 52 Americans hostage for 444 days, and diplomatic ties between the two countries were severed in 1980.

Iranian authorities have since turned the anniversary into an annual display of defiance against what they call Western “arrogance”.

“Crown of arrogance on an empty brain,” read one banner on Wednesday, showing a crown dripping with blood.

“America is the enemy regardless,” said Bagheri, a 35-year-old school principal who gave only her surname.

“It makes no difference who is in charge in the United States.”

headline: Turkiye's parliament set to ratify defence pact with Saudi Arabia, Pakistan as Houthi attacks mount
description: Agreement includes collective defence clause, committing Ankara to Riyadh’s defence but does not automatically require Turkish troop deployment
author: Reuters
article_text:
Turkiye’s parliament is set to ratify a defence pact on Wednesday with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan that includes a collective defence clause, committing NATO’s second-largest army to Riyadh’s defence as it faces attacks ​by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis.

Ratification gives Ankara a formal mutual defence obligation toward Saudi Arabia, but ‌it does not, on its own, send Turkish forces there. Deploying military personnel would require a separate mandate from parliament.

Turkiye submitted the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement — signed by the three countries in August — to parliament for ratification last month. Under the ​pact, whose key clause mirrors NATO’s Article 5, under which an attack on one member is ​treated as an attack on all, the parties plan to boost defence industry cooperation ⁠and military coordination, while creating deterrence against threats.

The pact was signed before the Houthis launched attacks against ​Saudi Arabia, and Wednesday’s vote comes after a senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran and Washington remain far from a deal to end their war, with Houthis stepping up attacks on Riyadh.

Officials had told Reuters last month that Turkiye’s contribution to Saudi Arabia was expected to be limited to military equipment, intelligence sharing, and weapons systems.

A lawmaker from Turkiye’s ruling ​party told Reuters earlier that Turkiye would also submit to parliament a mandate allowing for military personnel to ​be deployed to Saudi Arabia under the pact, but officials have said the scope of support for the kingdom would ‌be ⁠determined through collective consultations and in line with requests from Riyadh.

Analysts say Turkiye, which also has a robust defence industry, can help Saudi Arabia with technical support and combat expertise, as well as air defences and electronic warfare technologies. They say that Turkish troops, advisers and military personnel are expected to be deployed to ​help install and operate ​systems sent by Ankara ⁠once the planned deployment mandate is passed by parliament.

“I believe the Makkah alliance can be one of the first case studies of the concept that is called ‘defence ​as a service’, in which the supplier country not only provides equipment and ​platforms but ⁠also concepts, service, training, logistics as a whole, packaged together with political support and other layers of support,” Arda Mevlutoglu, a defence analyst, told Reuters.

Defence Minister Yasar Guler has said Turkiye did not see its troops engaging in ⁠combat or ​offensive operations against the Houthis.

Barin Kayaoglu, a professor of international relations ​at Ankara Social Sciences University and defence analyst, told Reuters the pact would also establish a certain level of interoperability between the ​allies as they operate similar systems and share expertise and technology.

headline: Democrats seize US Congress in rebuke of Trump
description: Republican strongholds fall as voters punish Trump over Iran war and high living costs
author: Reuters
article_text:
Democrats seized control of both the Senate and House of Representatives on Tuesday, scoring sweeping victories in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations as tens of millions of voters delivered a scathing rebuke to President Donald Trump.

Voters in conservative ​bastions who had propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats, fueled by deep frustration over the unpopular war with Iran, anxiety over the high cost of living and anger at ‌Trump’s stewardship of the country.

In Texas, the biggest Republican state, Democrats ended a decades-long losing streak in seismic fashion, winning a Senate seat and ousting three-term Governor Greg Abbott.

Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since the Great Depression nearly a century ago, and in South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, Democrats turned aside his hand-picked Senate candidate.

The results will usher in a new era of divided government in Washington, following two years in which the Republican-controlled Congress rarely exercised its power to rein in Trump.

Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump’s administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic ​Senate can block Trump’s nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise.

“There is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America,” said Chuck Schumer, the party’s Senate minority leader. “Americans voted for change, and now Democrats must ​deliver.”

Trump, who is barred by the US Constitution from seeking a third term, has exercised an iron grip on his party for most of the last decade. But the new balance of power in Washington may ⁠accelerate his lame-duck status, as attention turns toward the 2028 presidential race and potential successors begin competing for political influence in a post-Trump world.

Despite worries from Democrats that Trump might seek to overturn the election results, as he did in 2020, the president accepted the outcome, congratulating Democrats in ​an interview with Fox News. He also said he would work with Democrats on issues such as immigration, though he threatened to veto any “insane” bills they passed.

DEMOCRATIC WAVE

Democrats focused their campaign on corruption and affordability, blaming Trump’s tariff policy and the war with Iran for driving up costs while highlighting the ​billions of dollars the Trump family has made since he returned to the White House.

Republicans, led by Trump, attacked Democrats over culture war issues such as transgender rights while portraying their opponents as radical and extreme. But in poll after poll, voters made it clear they were far more concerned with pocketbook issues.

The Democratic wave flooded huge swaths of the country. Republicans lost ground in all but a handful of the approximately 2,100 counties where most votes had been counted, according to tallies compiled by Reuters and USA Today.

Democrats made gains in the richest counties and the poorest; in counties where more people have college degrees and where fewer do. Democrats’ advances were particularly sharp ​in heavily Latino counties, including the border counties of Texas that shifted toward Trump in 2024 and the agricultural towns of the Kansas prairie.

In Seward County, Kansas, home to one of America’s biggest beef processing plants and where about half of eligible voters are Hispanic, Democrat Adam Hamilton led ​incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall by 13 points, two years after Trump won the county by 39 points.

Democrats flipped more than two dozen House seats currently held by Republicans, locking in a majority. Democrats won all the closely contested House races that have been decided so far, and they won about a dozen races ‌in districts that Trump ⁠won by double digits two years ago.

An unprecedented Republican gambit to redraw several House districts to make them more favourable largely failed, with Democrats hanging on to most of the targeted seats.

Midterm elections are typically seen as a referendum on the sitting president, and Trump did little to disabuse voters of that notion. In the campaign’s final weeks, he held dozens of rallies, telling supporters repeatedly to “pretend I’m on the ballot.”

He also intervened in several Republican primaries earlier this year to ensure his preferred candidates reached the ballot, despite concerns from some Republicans that his choices carried significant liabilities.

The results will usher in a new era of divided government in Washington, following two years in which the Republican-controlled Congress rarely exercised its power to rein in Trump.

Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump’s administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic ​Senate can block Trump’s nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise.

“There is now a generational remake of the Senate map that is going to change America,” said Chuck Schumer, the party’s Senate minority leader. “Americans voted for change, and now Democrats must ​deliver.”

Trump, who is barred by the US Constitution from seeking a third term, has exercised an iron grip on his party for most of the last decade.
