headline: Vance blames Iran war for Republican election defeat, distances himself from Trump
description: US vice president questions war’s cost as Democrats seize control of Congress in sweeping midterm victories
author: Reuters
article_text:
US Vice President JD Vance distanced himself from President Donald Trump’s war on Iran on Wednesday, questioning its worth and ​blaming it entirely for a stinging electoral rebuke by voters ‌that delivered control of Congress to Democrats.

Vance’s extraordinary remarks in a post on X could further complicate Trump’s deliberations as he weighs whether to restart major combat operations ​against Iran, a step US officials have told Reuters is still under consideration.

They ​also raise questions about the political fortunes of senior Pentagon ⁠officials, most notably Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. Hegseth is already deeply unpopular ​in Congress, where some lawmakers are expected to seek his impeachment.

“The reason ​we lost is the war,” Vance said on X.

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, ​then do so.”

Vance also said an earlier recommendation to end the war ​was “sound advice.”

Democrats secured control of both the Senate and House of Representatives on Tuesday, scoring sweeping ‌victories ⁠in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations.

Voters in conservative bastions who had propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats, fueled by deep frustration over the ​war with Iran, anxiety ​over the high ⁠cost of living and anger at Trump’s stewardship of the country.

Vance sought to play down any difference of ​opinion with Trump, saying the president had also acknowledged ​that the ⁠Iran war cost Republicans the midterm elections on Tuesday. But Trump’s comments were far more measured, saying the Iran war was only one of multiple reasons.

“I ⁠did ​the right thing,” Trump told the Wall Street ​Journal. “I would have done it again.”

headline: European far right distances itself from Trump, blaming Iran war for Republicans' defeat
description: Most said Iran war and cost of living influenced US result
author: Reuters
article_text:
Europe’s far-right politicians on Wednesday began to distance themselves from Donald Trump following the Democrats’ victory in the US midterm elections – but mostly avoided directly criticising the president himself.

The realignment is notable as many of the leaders celebrated their ideological ties with Trump following ‌his victory in 2024, with some of them visiting Washington, DC, since then and receiving backing from his billionaire ally Elon Musk.

Jordan Bardella, leader of France’s National Rally, which most polls suggest could form the next government, typified the political shift.

Trump’s second term was less isolationist than his first from 2017 to 2021, Bardella said. “American intervention regarding Iran carries very heavy consequences” for economies around the world, ​he added, without mentioning Trump as being behind that intervention.

In Germany, Alice Weidel, co-leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, also attributed the loss to ​Iran. “Trump had promised his voters not to pursue an interventionist foreign policy … This broken promise has now come back to haunt ⁠the Republicans,” she told news outlet T-Online.

Trump acknowledged the war with Iran had played a role in his party’s losses but said he stood by his decision.

Cost of living pressures

In Italy, Matteo Salvini, leader of the far-right League party, which is part of the ruling coalition, said: “The American result was influenced above all by the wars, international tensions ​and the increase in the cost of living, the consequences of which fall directly on families.”

“The hope is that this vote can represent an acceleration towards the end of the conflicts and a return to peace.”

Roberto Vannacci, a former Italian general who leads the far-right Futuro Nazionale party, said the US result showed the political dangers of failing to deliver on electoral promises. Vannacci has ​previously expressed admiration for Trump’s “America First” brand of nationalist politics but has since criticised the president over foreign policy.

“Trump failed to live up to expectations, was unable to ​bring the war between Russia and Ukraine to an end and launched a war against Iran,” Vannacci told ANSA news agency, arguing that the resulting rise in energy prices and economic ‌and stock ⁠market turmoil had hurt the US middle class and contributed to the election result.

Ties with Trump could become an ‘Electoral liability’

Europe’s far-right leaders were distancing themselves from Trump for obvious political advantage, according to analyst Mujtaba Rahman, managing director of political risk consultancy Eurasia Group. “His growing unpopularity, particularly over the cost of living, risks turning what was once a political asset into an electoral liability,” he told Reuters.

Rahman said far-right leaders appeared to want it both ways: to reap the “ideological momentum of Trumpism” without being tarred by the “chaos ​and economic disruption of his presidency”.

“The risk ​is that Trump and his MAGA ⁠allies, who see Europe’s far right as ideological partners in their struggle against the European establishment, could respond by withdrawing their political support or even turning against them,” he added.

One of the few to play down the scale of the Republicans’ defeat was ​Dan Dungaciu, vice-president of the opposition hard-right Alliance for Uniting Romanians, who argued that reports of Trump’s “political death” were “greatly exaggerated”. ​He added, “Donald Trump does ⁠not automatically become a powerless president. Instead, he moves from a presidency backed by Republican majorities to one in which the executive and Congress will check each other much more intensely.”

In Spain, the leader of the far-right party Vox, Santiago Abascal, made little attempt to temper his move away from Trump, telling reporters he was “in Spain and not in Michigan”.

“I care ⁠quite little ​about what happens in other places,” said Abascal, who has in the past touted his alliance with ​Trump and the MAGA movement.

Rupert Lowe, leader of the far-right Restore Britain party, also blamed the decision to attack Iran for the Republicans’ defeat, calling it a “catastrophic mistake.” He added, “What has this war achieved? Absolutely ​nothing of worth.” Lowe did not, though, include in his lengthy X post the name of the president who launched the war.

headline: Petrol, diesel prices cut for third consecutive day
description: Government reduces petrol by Rs7.06 and diesel by Rs3.71 per litre; new rates applicable for November 5 only
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The federal government on Wednesday reduced the prices of petrol and high-speed diesel (HSD) for the third consecutive day, announcing cuts of Rs7.06 and Rs3.71 per litre, respectively, for November 5.

According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol has been reduced from Rs369.06 to Rs362 per litre, while diesel will now cost Rs387.81 per litre, down from Rs391.52.

The revised prices will take effect at midnight and remain applicable for one day, November 5, 2026.

The notification said the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) revised petroleum prices in accordance with the pricing mechanism issued by the federal government.

The adjustments are linked to international petroleum prices and take into account changes in global markets, Platts rates, premiums and other incidental costs, according to the Petroleum Division.

The latest reduction follows two consecutive cuts announced earlier this week.

On Tuesday, the government reduced the price of petrol by Rs5.45 per litre to Rs369.06 and diesel by Rs3.68 to Rs391.52.

A day earlier, on Monday, petrol became cheaper by Rs3.40 per litre to Rs374.51, while the price of diesel was reduced by Rs7.76 to Rs395.20.

The government has been determining petroleum prices on a daily basis in response to the Middle East crisis, while keeping rates unchanged on Saturdays and Sundays.
